title: Highest-Protein Fish: A Clear Ranking per 100 Grams

seo.title: Highest-Protein Fish per 100 Grams
seo.meta_description: Compare cooked tuna, mackerel, trout, swordfish, cod and salmon by protein, calories and serving, with clear mercury context.
seo.search_intent: Compare cooked fish by protein without mixing canned and fresh products.

excerpt: Yellowfin tuna separates itself at the top, but mackerel, trout, swordfish, cod and salmon are much closer than most rankings suggest. Fat, calories, mercury and sodium often differ more than protein.
content_html:
Fish is already a protein-rich category, so a ranking can make small differences look bigger than they really are. To keep the comparison fair, the main table uses cooked fish. Canned fish sits separately because oil, salt and draining change the product substantially.

Cooked fish on the same scale

FishProtein/100 gCalories/100 g
Yellowfin tuna29.2 g130
Atlantic mackerel23.9 g262
Farmed rainbow trout23.8 g168
Swordfish23.5 g172
Wild rainbow trout22.9 g150
Atlantic cod22.8 g105
Farmed Atlantic salmon22.1 g206
Haddock20.0 g90

Mackerel, trout, swordfish and cod differ by only about 1 gram of protein per 100 grams. Cod and mackerel, meanwhile, differ by well over 150 calories. That tells you where the more meaningful nutritional differences often are.

Tuna is the clear protein outlier

Cooked yellowfin tuna provides about 29.2 g protein and 130 calories per 100 g. It is lean and highly protein-dense.

But “tuna” is not one mercury category. FDA/EPA advice places canned light tuna in “Best Choices,” albacore/white tuna in “Good Choices,” and bigeye tuna in “Choices to Avoid” for pregnant or breastfeeding people and children. Species matters more than the generic name.

Mackerel and salmon bring much more fat with similar protein

Atlantic mackerel provides about 23.9 g protein and 262 calories/100 g; farmed Atlantic salmon about 22.1 g and 206 calories. Cod provides a similar 22.8 g protein with only 105 calories.

The extra energy in mackerel and salmon largely comes from fat, including EPA and DHA omega-3s. A higher calorie count is therefore not automatically a nutritional disadvantage.

Trout sits right in the middle

Farmed rainbow trout is around 23.8 g protein/100 g and wild rainbow trout around 22.9 g. A 5-ounce / 142 g serving provides roughly 34 and 33 g protein — a very small practical difference.

Swordfish stands out for mercury, not protein

Swordfish provides about 23.5 g protein/100 g, almost the same as trout and mackerel. FDA/EPA classifies it as a “Choice to Avoid” for pregnant or breastfeeding people and young children because of mercury.

Cod and haddock are very lean

Cod provides 22.8 g protein and 105 calories/100 g; haddock roughly 20 g and 90 calories. That makes both especially efficient when the question is protein per calorie.

Salted cod is another product entirely: curing removes water and greatly increases sodium. Even after desalting, it should not be treated as identical to simply cooked fresh cod.

Canned sardines and anchovies look more concentrated

Drained canned sardines in oil provide about 24.6 g protein/100 g; drained anchovies can approach 28.9 g/100 g. Lower water content raises the concentration.

Serving size brings the numbers back to earth. Twenty grams of anchovies provides about 5.8 g protein, not 28.9 g. Sardines with edible bones also contribute substantial calcium, while anchovies are very high in sodium.

What a normal serving provides

FishServingProtein
Cooked tuna5 oz / 142 g41 g
Mackerel5 oz / 142 g34 g
Trout5 oz / 142 g34 g
Cod5 oz / 142 g32 g
Salmon5 oz / 142 g31 g
Canned sardines3.75 oz can / ~106 g~26 g

“White” versus “oily” predicts fat better than protein

Cod and salmon provide 22.8 and 22.1 g protein/100 g, almost identical. The larger difference is fat: salmon commonly has more than 10 g/100 g while cod is near 1 g.

The choice is usually about more than one gram of protein

Tuna sits near the top for protein concentration, but many fish cluster around 20–24 g/100 g. When the protein numbers are this close, omega-3 content, mercury, calcium, sodium, cost and preference often matter more.

Sources

Food values come from USDA FoodData Central. Mercury advice comes from FDA/EPA Advice about Eating Fish.

faq.question: Which fish has the most protein?
faq.answer: Among the cooked fish compared here, yellowfin tuna is about 29.2 g/100 g. Mackerel, trout, swordfish and cod cluster around 22.8–23.9 g.

faq.question: Does salmon have less protein than tuna?
faq.answer: Yes in these examples: about 22.1 g/100 g versus 29.2 g for yellowfin tuna. Salmon contains much more fat, including omega-3s.

faq.question: Which fish are highest in mercury?
faq.answer: FDA/EPA places swordfish and bigeye tuna among the choices to avoid for pregnant or breastfeeding people and children.
